I think the majority of people will disagree with me, but I think Zelda will.

Don't get me wrong, it'll sell rather well. It's Zelda, there's no way it won't sell. And it'll sell better than other, perhaps more deserving games. But I think it's going to be very disappointing to the devotees.

The typical Zelda fanboy wants a very tight story: after all, they fight over the lore and what is canon and the official Zelda timeline and stuff like that. An open world is going to further dilute that linear path in the same way that Zelda games in general have gotten worse the more optional stuff they've thrown into it. Platform limitations in the past games forced the Zelda franchise to keep constrained and disciplined and, starting with Ocarina, there was more room to stretch their legs.

I guess my prediction is that they're now so bottomheavy on optional stuff that the open world is the only way to express it, thus the world of Hyrule is going to feel very barren and unsatisfying. There will be devoted fans that give it 10/10 GOTY status on Metacritic, and a dishonest gaming media will likely follow suit, but I think most people that buy and play it will not like it and think there is something wrong with them instead of the game. At least that's how I felt, playing both Skyward Sword and Twilight Princess.

Paper Mario Color Splash is pretty much 100% certain to flop.

Why?

Because it's taken one of the most hated Paper Mario games and expanded on that rather than what the fans, critics and audience actually want.

Yes, Sticker Star did okay. But that was on the back of hype, the best selling game in the franchise and a fandom willing to give it a shot.

People won't make that mistake twice. Heck, Mario & Luigi Paper Jam actually bombed hard because it pretty much entirely stuck to Sticker Star's ideas and character list. The series went from selling a few million copies (Dream Team) to basically not breaking a million, because Sticker Star was that utterly despised by the fans.

Color Splash is also gonna sell poorly because:

It's on a failing console in the Wii U, which has a very limited audience in general. Mario platformers aren't/are barely breaking 5 million copies sold on it. Mario RPGs in their best days sell about 4 million copies on a system selling about 80 million units.

It's also released at a time where the Wii U has basically been abandoned, the NX is around the corner and people are more hyped for the likes of Pokemon Sun and Moon.

Either way, I'll be surprised if it sells more than a million copies, and am basically predicting it to fail as hard Star Fox Zero did.

Why You Shouldn't Write an Application Builder (and What to Do Instead)

This is my own blog. It's not meant as spam, but if posting your own articles here is strictly verboten, someone let me know and I'll take it down.

Otherwise, I'd love to hear your thoughts! Has anyone else been tasked to write an application builder? I had to help build one at a recent job, and a guy on my team said (woefully) that he'd built numerous ones. Seems like this is a common idea among non-technical managers, but I've never met a developer who thought it was a good idea.

Any such application builder is really just implementing a new visual programming language. This means creating application builders comes with all the associated pros and cons of creating new programming languages but unfortunately most people don't realize that.
Exactly. There inevitably comes a need for custom logic, and so the app builder has to become more configurable. Eventually it becomes so configurable that's it's Turing complete.

I came to the same conclusion 15 years ago when working in web dev. Your customer wants to run their own web site, so you build them a CMS. They want it to be more flexible so you add features. They want to be able to script and style and alter the layout and and and... you've looped right back around and what they really want is Apache + PHP.
Yep. But they never want to learn it :/
